DOCUMENT:
Evaluation of the First-Year Peer Mentoring Scheme, 2025-26
Student Success Unit, Northbridge University, July 2026

1. Purpose
Continuation from first to second year is a key regulatory and financial measure for the University. In 2024-25, 13% of full-time first-year undergraduates did not continue into their second year. In 2025-26 the University piloted a peer mentoring scheme for first-year students. This report evaluates the pilot and recommends whether it should be extended.

2. The scheme
Students in their second or third year were recruited and trained as mentors, and each was matched with up to eight first-year mentees from the same faculty. Mentors held a group session every fortnight during the first term and were available for one-to-one meetings throughout the year. Mentors were paid £1,200 for the year. They attended a half-day training session in September covering listening skills, signposting to support services and safeguarding, and were supported by a coordinator in each faculty. First-year students were invited to opt in during welcome week.

Recruiting mentors proved harder than expected. We advertised 200 mentor posts and filled 155, which allowed us to offer places to 1,240 first-year students (155 mentors with eight mentees each). Mentee places were taken up within the first two weeks and a waiting list was closed at 300 names.

3. Who took part
Of the 4,100 full-time first-year students, 1,240 took part. Mentees were more likely than other first-years to be living in university halls (78% compared with 52%) and were somewhat more likely to have entered with higher tariff qualifications. They were similar to non-mentees in age and gender.

4. Results
Table 1. Continuation into second year, 2025-26 entrants
Group | Students | Continuing to year two | Continuation rate
Mentored | 1,240 | 1,166 | 94.0%
Not mentored | 2,860 | 2,460 | 86.0%
All first-years | 4,100 | 3,626 | 88.4%

Mentored students were eight percentage points more likely to continue into their second year. Overall continuation rose to 88.4%, from 87% the previous year.

The eight-point gap is clear evidence that peer mentoring improves continuation. Applied to the 1,240 mentees, it means that around 99 students continued who would otherwise have left. At £9,250 a year in tuition fee income, these students are worth about £1.2 million to the University in their second year alone.

Mentees rated the scheme 4.3 out of 5 in the end-of-year survey, and many commented that it helped them settle in and find out about support services. Mentors reported that the role improved their own confidence and employability.

5. Costs
The pilot cost £186,000 for mentor pay, £12,000 for training and £18,000 for coordination, a total of £216,000, or about £174 per mentee.

6. Recommendation
We recommend that from 2026-27 peer mentoring becomes a standard part of the first-year experience, with every full-time first-year student allocated a mentor automatically rather than opting in. On the pilot's costs of about £174 per mentee, this would cost around £714,000 a year for 4,100 students. On the pilot's results, it would raise continuation to around 94% across the whole first-year cohort, a gain of over 200 continuing students a year, and the fee income retained would cover the cost several times over.

7. Conclusion
The pilot has shown that peer mentoring improves continuation by eight percentage points, pays for itself many times over, and is valued by mentees and mentors alike. Extending it to all first-year students is a clear opportunity to improve outcomes and secure the University's continuation performance.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [arithmetic] at: "these students are worth about £1.2 million to the University in their second year alone" -- 99 students x £9,250 = £915,750, about £0.9 million, not £1.2 million.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "The eight-point gap is clear evidence that peer mentoring improves continuation." -- Students opted in, and the document reports mentees were more likely to live in halls (78% vs 52%) and to have higher entry qualifications, both associated with continuation. Self-selection and these confounders mean the gap does not show that mentoring caused higher continuation.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "with every full-time first-year student allocated a mentor automatically rather than opting in" -- Scaling to 4,100 students at eight mentees per mentor needs about 513 mentors, but the document reports the University could fill only 155 of 200 advertised posts. The recommendation and costing assume mentor supply scales and never address the stated recruitment constraint (nor that automatically enrolled students may benefit less than volunteers).

REVIEW:
# Review: First-Year Peer Mentoring Evaluation, 2025-26

**Overall:** The recommendation may well be right, but the report doesn't support it as strongly as the author claims. The data are complete, and the pilot costs are internally consistent. The central causal claim and the financial case both have serious problems, and one figure is wrong.

## 1. The 8-point gap is not evidence that the scheme works (major)

Students opted in, and mentee places filled within two weeks. The mentees were therefore self-selected, and the report itself shows they differ from other students:

- 78% lived in halls, against 52% of non-mentees.
- They had somewhat higher entry tariffs.

Both factors are associated with better continuation on their own. The report matches on age and gender only, which are the two characteristics least likely to matter here. Motivation, which is likely the biggest confounder, can't be observed at all.

There is also an early-leaver effect. Students who left in the first two weeks couldn't have been mentees, but they count in the non-mentored group.

"Complete and objective" outcome data fix measurement error. They do nothing about selection bias.

## 2. The report's own year-on-year data suggest a much smaller effect

Last year's continuation was 87%. At that rate, 4,100 students would give about 3,567 continuers, but the actual figure was 3,626. That is about **59** extra students, not 99, and it ignores any other year-on-year change.

Non-mentees continued at 86%, below last year's cohort-wide 87%. That pattern fits the scheme drawing already-likely continuers into the mentored group, rather than creating new ones.

## 3. The £1.2 million figure is wrong (arithmetic)

99 × £9,250 = **about £916,000**, not £1.2 million. £1.2m would need about 130 students.

It is also gross fee income, not net of the cost of educating those students. Even corrected, the figure is only valid if the whole 8-point gap is causal.

## 4. The roll-out projection rests on untested assumptions

- **Opt-in vs automatic.** The effect was measured on students who chose to take part. Nothing shows it carries over to students allocated a mentor by default, who are likely less engaged.
- **Mentor supply.** The pilot advertised 200 posts and filled 155. At eight mentees each, 4,100 students need about **513 mentors**, more than three times the pilot's number. The report doesn't address whether that pool exists, or whether pay would need to rise.
- **Linear cost scaling.** £174 × 4,100 = £714,000 is arithmetically correct. But training, coordination and recruitment costs won't scale linearly, and the figure leaves out any extra recruitment effort or management overhead.
- **The 94% projection.** This simply applies the mentee rate to everyone. It assumes no selection effect at all.

A useful reframing is that the roll-out breaks even at about **77 additional continuing students** (£714k ÷ £9,250), or roughly a 1.9-point rise in cohort continuation. That is a far more defensible claim than "pays for itself several times over," though it still needs a credible estimate of the true effect.

## 5. Qualitative evidence is weaker than presented

- No survey response rate is given.
- Students who withdrew are unlikely to have completed an end-of-year survey, so the 4.3/5 reflects survivors.
- There are no engagement data, such as how many sessions mentees actually attended, so no dose-response check is possible.

## 6. A timing question

The report is dated July 2026, but continuation "to the start of the second year" can't normally be known until enrolment in September/October. The report should explain what was actually measured (pre-enrolment intentions, re-registration, something else?). If it's not a final enrolment outcome, the "complete and objective" claim needs qualifying.

## 7. Claims in the author's summary that don't hold up

| Author's claim | Assessment |
|---|---|
| "Shows the scheme works" | Unsupported; selection bias is unaddressed |
| "~£1.2 million" | Arithmetic error; about £916k at most |
| "Pays for itself several times over" | Only if the effect is fully causal and generalises |
| "Costing built from actual pilot spend" | True, but that's the weakness: it assumes linear scaling |
| "One of the best-evidenced initiatives" | Overclaim for an observational, self-selected comparison |

## Recommended fixes

1. Re-run the comparison with adjustment (regression or matching on tariff, residence, faculty, prior attainment, widening participation markers) and report the adjusted effect with confidence intervals.
2. Use the 300-name waiting list as a comparison group, since those students were motivated enough to apply.
3. Correct the £1.2m figure and present a range of scenarios (e.g., effect of 2, 4 and 8 points), net of marginal cost.
4. Cost the roll-out bottom-up, including mentor supply, pay, and coordination capacity.
5. Report survey response rates and mentoring engagement data.
6. Clarify the continuation measurement date.
7. Consider a **phased or randomised roll-out** in 2026-27, such as randomising allocation within faculties, so the University gets real causal evidence before committing £714k a year.
8. Soften the language in sections 4 and 7 from "has shown" to "is consistent with."
